nuance.analogy: To collate is like sorting a shuffled deck of cards into order so you can see which cards match and which are missing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin collatus, past participle of conferre, to bring together or compare, from com- 'together' and latus, the past participle of ferre 'to bear'.
common_mistakes: Confusing collate with correlate, which means showing a statistical relationship.
Using collate for ordinary sorting in casual speech, where put together or sort is more natural.

core.definition: The spiritual union of all believers in Christ, living and dead, sharing in God's life and praying for one another.

pronunciation.tip: In 'communion' the stress is on 'MYOON' and the ending is a quick 'yun'. In the phrase, 'of' reduces to 'uv', and 'saints' gets the stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent; suggests unity and fellowship across time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear this phrase mainly in church, especially from the Apostles' Creed, which many say weekly. It is not casual speech, and outside Christian circles most people will not know it. Avoid confusing it with the Communion service.

distinctions.note: Communion alone often means the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; communion of saints refers to the fellowship of believers.
Fellowship is the shared life of a local group; communion of saints is universal and includes the departed.
The church is the body of believers; the communion of saints stresses their unity and shared life.

collocations: believe in the communion of saints
fellowship of the communion of saints
the Church and the communion of saints

examples.everyday: When we say the Creed, I always think about the communion of saints, the people who prayed in this church before me.
examples.professional: This course explores how the communion of saints shapes Christian ideas of prayer, memory, and the afterlife.
examples.analytical: The doctrine of the communion of saints holds that death does not sever the bond among those united in Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a family that stays one even when some members are in another room.
nuance.etymology: Latin communio sanctorum, which can mean both fellowship of holy persons and sharing in holy things.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the sacrament of Communion.
Pronouncing 'communion' as 'kuh-MYOO-nee-on'; the ending is 'yun'.
Dropping the plural s: say 'saints', not 'saint'.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase itself is not in the Bible, but the idea rests on Greek koinonia, 'fellowship,' and hagioi, 'saints.' 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 describes the church as one body whose members share one another's joys and sufferings. Hebrews 12:1 pictures believers surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses. Revelation 7:9-10 shows a multitude from every nation worshiping before the throne.

traditions.view: The Church includes the faithful on earth, souls being purified, and the saints in heaven, all united and able to help one another by prayer.
The Church is one living body on earth and in heaven. The living and departed pray for each other, especially in the Divine Liturgy.

Most affirm the communion of saints as the unity of all believers in Christ, and the Apostles' Creed is widely used. Many deny that departed saints should be invoked, though some, like Anglicans and Lutherans, remember them with thanks.

senses.definition: The science and technology of machines that see, concerned with the theory for building artificial systems that obtain information from images, such as a video sequence, views from multiple cameras, or multi-dimensional data from a medical scanner.

conversation.text: Computer vision teaches machines to interpret images and video.
Our computer vision model inspects welds on the production line.
Computer vision is how your phone finds all the photos of your dog.

core.definition: The field of AI concerned with enabling computers to interpret and understand images and video, such as recognizing objects or faces.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on PYOO, and vision is pronounced with a zh sound, like 'measure', followed by a reduced 'un'. Do not say it as 'VIZH-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a respected research field with many practical applications, so people usually talk about it with interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term for both the research field and the technology it produces, such as face unlock or quality inspection in factories. In job postings and team talk, people often say 'CV' for computer vision, which can confuse people who read it as curriculum vitae. A natural reply to 'What do you work on?' is 'Mostly computer vision, for medical imaging.'

distinctions.note: Image processing transforms or enhances images, such as sharpening or filtering, while computer vision extracts meaning and understanding from them.
Machine learning is a general set of methods for learning from data, while computer vision is an application area that often uses machine learning on images.

examples.everyday: My phone uses computer vision to recognize faces when I unlock it.
examples.professional: Our computer vision team is training a model to flag defects on the assembly line in real time.
examples.analytical: Computer vision raises philosophical questions about what it means to see, since a machine may classify images without any understanding of them.

nuance.analogy: Computer vision is like teaching a machine to glance at a photo and say what matters in it, the way a radiologist reads a scan.
nuance.etymology: 'Computer' comes from compute; 'vision' comes from Latin visio, from videre, 'to see'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing vision as VIZH-un with the wrong stress, or as VIJ-un.
Using CV without context, since in many American workplaces it can also mean a resume.

senses.definition: A food item prepared very sweet, frequently decorated in fine detail, and often preserved with sugar, such as a candy, sweetmeat, fruit preserve, pastry, or cake.
senses.example: The table was covered with all sorts of tempting confections.

senses.definition: The act or process of confecting; the process of making, compounding, or preparing something.
The result of such a process; something made up or confected; a concoction.
senses.example: The defense attorney maintained that the charges were a confection of the local police.

senses.definition: A preparation of medicine sweetened with sugar, honey, syrup, or the like; an electuary.
An artistic, musical, or literary work taken as frivolous, amusing, or contrived; a composition of a light nature.
Something, such as a garment or a decoration, that is very elaborate, delicate, or luxurious, usually also impractical or non-utilitarian.
senses.example: Her gown was a marvelous confection of lace and tulle.

senses.definition: To make into a confection, prepare as a confection.

words.etymology: From Middle English *confescioun*, borrowed from Old French *confeccion* (French *confection*), borrowed from Latin *confectio*, from *cōnfectus*, past participle of *cōnficiō* (“prepare”), from *con-* (“with”) + *faciō* (“to make, do”).

core.definition: A sweet food, such as a candy, pastry, or cake, often elaborately decorated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FEK, and the ending is the sound 'shun', not 'chun'. The first vowel is the reduced schwa, so the word sounds like 'kun' not 'con'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting something delicate, fancy, and appealing; it can sound slightly exaggerated in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confection mostly in writing, menus, and descriptions of fancy desserts, such as 'a lemon confection' at a bakery. In everyday speech people say dessert, candy, or sweet. Confectionery refers to the shop or the category of candy, so do not use confection for the store.

distinctions.note: Candy is the everyday word for sweets, while confection suggests something elaborate or artful.
Dessert means any sweet served at the end of a meal, while a confection can be a standalone sweet item.
Confectionery is the shop or the whole category of sweets, while confection is one item.

collocations: a light confection of cream and fruit

examples.everyday: That lemon cake at the farmers market is a real confection, with little sugar roses on top.
examples.professional: The pastry team wants a seasonal confection for the spring menu that can be plated in under two minutes.
examples.analytical: The poem describes the dessert as a confection of spun sugar and longing, implying that beauty is always fragile.

nuance.analogy: Like a wedding cake, which is built to look delicate and perfect, with every layer carefully arranged.
nuance.etymology: From Latin confectio, 'a making up, preparation,' from conficere, 'to make up, prepare,' from com- and facere 'to make.'
common_mistakes: Using confection for a candy store, when the store is a confectionery.
Mispronouncing the ending as 'chun' instead of 'shun'.
Using it for everyday candy, when candy is the more natural everyday word.

senses.definition: In a conniving manner.

words.etymology: From *conniving* + *ly*.

core.definition: In a scheming way, secretly planning or cooperating with others to do something wrong, or deliberately overlooking it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'NYVE'. The -ing is a short 'ing', and the final -ly is a long 'lee' sound, not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a sly, complicit manner.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly see 'connivingly' in literary or descriptive writing, and it is rare in conversation. In speech, people would say 'with a sly look' or 'scheming'. Use it to describe a look, smile or manner, as in 'she smiled connivingly'.

distinctions.note: Slyly means cleverly or secretly in general; connivingly suggests a plot involving collaboration or deliberate overlooking of wrongdoing.
Deceitfully emphasizes lying or cheating; connivingly emphasizes a scheming, complicit manner.

examples.everyday: She grinned connivingly when she saw the surprise party plans on my phone.
examples.professional: The vendor nodded connivingly at the inflated invoice, and nobody on the call questioned it.
examples.analytical: The novel's officials watch the abuses connivingly, and their silence makes them complicit.

nuance.analogy: Like two kids sharing a glance over a stolen cookie, the look says they both know and agree.
nuance.etymology: From connive, from Latin connivere, 'to close the eyes, wink at', with the adverbial suffix -ingly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable 'lie' instead of 'lee'.
Using it to mean 'cleverly' in a positive way; it usually implies a negative plot.

senses.definition: The act of consulting.
A conference for the exchange of information and advice.
An appointment or meeting with a professional person, such as a doctor.

words.etymology: From Middle French *consultation*, from Latin *consultatio*.

core.definition: A meeting with a professional, such as a doctor, lawyer or expert, to get advice or information; also a formal exchange of views.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -TAY- syllable, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The middle vowels reduce to a weak uh sound, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional; it sounds respectful and businesslike, and can feel impersonal in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use consultation mostly for a planned meeting with an expert, especially a doctor, lawyer or consultant, as in 'I have a consultation with my dentist.' In everyday talk people more often say 'appointment' or 'visit.' In business, a consultation can also mean a process of gathering input from stakeholders before a decision.

distinctions.note: An appointment is any scheduled time; a consultation is specifically a meeting to get expert advice.
A consultancy is a firm that sells expert advice; a consultation is a single meeting or act of asking for advice.
Advice is the guidance itself; a consultation is the meeting or process in which you receive it.

examples.everyday: I have a consultation with my dentist at ten tomorrow, so I'll be late to lunch.
examples.professional: After the model review, we'll hold a consultation with the product team before we change the threshold.
examples.analytical: Democratic consultation is valuable not only for its outcomes but because it recognizes the dignity of those affected by a decision.

nuance.analogy: Think of it as a structured conversation with an expert, not a casual chat with a friend.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consultare, to consult frequently, from consulere, to take counsel.
common_mistakes: Using consultation for a casual talk with friends; say 'advice' or 'talk' instead.
Stressing the first syllable or the -SUL- part; the main stress is on -TAY-.
Saying 'consult to a doctor'; the verb takes no preposition in 'consult a doctor'.

senses.definition: Sincerely penitent or feeling regret or sorrow, especially for one’s own actions.
A contrite person; a penitent.

words.etymology: From Middle English *contrit*, from Old French *contrit*, from Latin *contrītus*, perfect passive participle of *conterō* (“grind, bruise”), from *con-* + *terō* (“rub, wear away”).

core.definition: Feeling sincere regret or sorrow for something wrong you have done, and wanting to make it right.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TRITE, and the first syllable is a weak schwa, so do not say KON-trite. Americans rhotic-pronounce the r, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes sincere remorse and is a compliment to someone who admits fault. It can sound slightly stiff in casual speech, where people more often say sorry or feel bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contrite mostly in writing, in news reports, apologies and formal or religious speech, and when describing someone's tone. In everyday talk, 'I feel terrible about it' or 'I'm really sorry' is more natural. A typical phrase is 'He was contrite about the mistake,' and a good reply to a contrite apology is 'Thanks, I appreciate that.'

distinctions.note: Remorseful is more common in everyday speech and stresses a painful feeling of guilt, while contrite stresses the sincere wish to make amends and is often used for formal apologies.
Sorry is the everyday word and can mean mere regret, such as being sorry about the weather. Contrite implies that you are truly accepting blame for your own wrongdoing.

examples.everyday: She looked really contrite after she forgot my birthday, and she bought me lunch to make up for it.
examples.professional: He sent a contrite email to the whole team after missing the release deadline and took ownership of the delay.
examples.analytical: Many spiritual writers argue that a contrite heart, rather than outward ritual, is what makes repentance genuine.

nuance.analogy: Contrite is like a bent-over apology: the body language shows that the person feels the weight of what they did.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contritus, 'worn down, crushed,' the past participle of conterere, 'to rub together, bruise.'
common_mistakes: Using contrite for simple sadness, such as 'I am contrite that it rained'; use sorry or disappointed instead.
Pronouncing the first syllable as KON-, when the stress is on the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, contrite translates Hebrew words meaning 'crushed' or 'broken' (dakka', from daka', 'to crush'; and nakhe', 'smitten, afflicted'), describing a heart that is humbled and broken before God. Psalm 51:17 speaks of a broken and contrite heart that God will not despise. Isaiah 57:15 says God dwells with the one who is of a contrite and lowly spirit. Psalm 34:18 says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

senses.definition: Of or relating to Corinth.
Of the Corinthian order.
Elaborate, ornate.
Debauched in character or practice; impure.
Being a sporting event (originally in horse racing and yachting) restricted to gentleman amateurs.
An inhabitant or a resident of Corinth, and its suburbs.
An inhabitant, a resident of; a thing that originates from Corinthia.
An accomplished amateur athlete.
A sailboat owner who helms their own boat in competitive racing.
A worldly, fashionable person, accepted in society though possibly dissolute.

core.definition: Two New Testament letters written by the apostle Paul to the Christian church in Corinth, a city in ancient Greece: First and Second Corinthians.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RIN, not on the first or last syllable. The th is voiceless, as in thin, and many Americans say the ending as shuhnz, so either pronunciation is acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name for a biblical book, with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say First Corinthians or 1 Corinthians, and Second Corinthians or 2 Corinthians, in church and Bible study. Use the plural form, Corinthians, to refer to the book, and Corinth, the city, for the place. Speakers in the Catholic and Protestant traditions use the same book names, so the term is safe in any church setting.

distinctions.note: Corinth is the ancient Greek city, while Corinthians refers to the letters Paul wrote to the church there, or to the people of that church.
Corinthian as an adjective can describe a style of classical column or, informally, a dashing person, so it has other meanings besides the biblical letters.

examples.everyday: We're reading First Corinthians at Bible study on Wednesday, so bring your Bible.
examples.professional: For the seminary course, students should compare Paul's rhetoric in Second Corinthians with his argument in Galatians.
examples.analytical: The Corinthian correspondence shows Paul negotiating factional disputes in a congregation he had founded, especially in First Corinthians.

nuance.analogy: The two letters are like a pastor's replies to a congregation's specific questions, written in response to real problems rather than as a general textbook.
nuance.etymology: Named after the city of Corinth in Greece, where the church addressed in the letters was located.
common_mistakes: Saying Corinthian for the book, when the standard name is Corinthians (plural).
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in kor-in-THEE-ans, when the stress is on RIN.
nuance.biblical_note: First and Second Corinthians are two letters from Paul to the church in Corinth (Greek: ekklēsia, meaning assembly or church). Key passages: 1 Corinthians 1:10-12 describes factions in the church, 1 Corinthians 13 is Paul's famous chapter on love, 1 Corinthians 15 addresses the resurrection of the dead, and 2 Corinthians 5:17 speaks of anyone in Christ becoming a new creation.

senses.definition: Dampening the cyclical fluctuations due to the business cycle in an economy.
Moving in the direction opposite to that of the overall state of an economy.
senses.example: The unemployment rate is countercyclical in the sense that it rises when economic growth is low and vice versa.

core.definition: Moving against the economy's business cycle, such as government spending that rises during recessions to soften downturns.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, KOWN, with a secondary stress on SY. The 'cycl' part is pronounced like 'sy-kl', and the last syllable is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in economics, finance, and policy discussions, such as in news reports about the Federal Reserve or government stimulus. It is rarely used in casual conversation. People say 'countercyclical policy' or 'countercyclical spending' to describe actions that counter economic trends.

distinctions.note: Procyclical means moving in the same direction as the economy, amplifying booms and busts, which is the opposite of countercyclical.
Anticyclical is a less common variant with the same meaning, and countercyclical is the preferred term in American economics.
Stabilizing is a general word for reducing volatility, while countercyclical specifically refers to acting against the business cycle.

examples.everyday: The news says the government wants countercyclical spending to help us if the economy slows down.
examples.professional: Our risk model needs a countercyclical buffer so the bank can absorb losses when credit conditions tighten.
examples.analytical: A central question in macroeconomic theory is whether countercyclical fiscal policy truly reduces the amplitude of recessions.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermostat that turns on the heater when the room gets cold, countercyclical policy pushes back against the swings.
nuance.etymology: From counter- (against) plus cyclical (relating to a cycle), from Greek kyklos (circle).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with procyclical, which means the opposite.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'coun-ter-SIGH-cli-cal' instead of 'KOWN-ter-SY-klih-kuhl'.

senses.definition: Believable or plausible.
senses.example: credible alibi

senses.definition: Dependable, trustworthy, or reliable.
senses.example: credible sources

senses.definition: Authentic or convincing.
senses.example: credible acting

words.etymology: From Middle English *credible*, borrowed from Middle French *credible*, from Latin *crēdibilis* (“worthy of belief”), from *crēdō* (“believe”); see credit.

core.definition: Believable and trustworthy enough that people can reasonably accept it as true or rely on it as reliable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, KRED. The ending -ible is said as a syllabic 'bul' with no vowel between b and l, so it sounds like 'bul', not 'bell' or 'ble'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing a source, claim, or person; negative when used with not, as in not credible, to dismiss an excuse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say credible for sources, evidence, threats, and witnesses, and they often use it in news, legal, and workplace contexts. In casual speech people more often say believable or make sense, so credible may sound a bit formal in a friendly chat. The phrase not very credible is a common polite way to say an excuse is weak.

distinctions.note: Credible describes something worthy of belief, while credulous describes a person who believes too easily.
Believable is more casual and common in speech; credible sounds more formal and often implies evidence or reliability.
Plausible means it sounds reasonable, but credible means it is trustworthy enough to rely on.

antonyms: incredible in the sense of unbelievable

examples.everyday: Their excuse didn't sound very credible, so I stopped believing them.
examples.professional: We need a credible estimate of the migration cost before we present anything to the board.
examples.analytical: A theory is credible when it survives serious attempts to falsify it, not merely when it is attractive.

nuance.analogy: A credible source is like a sturdy bridge: you can walk across it with confidence because it has been tested.
nuance.etymology: From Latin credibilis, meaning believable, from credere, to believe.
common_mistakes: Confusing credible with creditable, which means deserving praise or respect.
Pronouncing the ending as 'ible' like 'possible' with a full vowel; the ending is a syllabic 'bul'.

senses.definition: To pick or take someone or something (from a larger group).
To gather, collect.

To select (animals, plants, humans, etc) from a group and then kill (them) in a controlled manner, typically to reduce the numbers of the group or remove group members who have an undesirable characteristic.
(Should we delete this redundant sense?) To kill (an animal, person, etc), for any reason.
To lay off in order to reduce the numbers of; get rid of.
senses.example: The company culled more employees this month.

senses.definition: To selectively not render or process certain objects, such as polygons.
senses.example: back-face culling

senses.definition: A selection.
An organized killing of selected animals.
An individual animal selected to be killed, or item of produce to be discarded.
A lobster having only one claw.
A piece unfit for inclusion within a larger group; an inferior specimen.
The act of laying off employees.

words.etymology: From Middle English *cullen*, *cuilen*, *coilen*, from Old French *cuillir* (“collect, gather, select”), from Latin *colligō* (“gather together”).

core.definition: To select and remove certain animals or items from a group, often by killing them to control numbers.

pronunciation.tip: One short syllable with the same vowel as 'cut' or 'hut'. End with a clear l sound.

nuance.connotation: negative; it sounds clinical and sometimes harsh, especially about animals or people.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'cull' appears mostly in farming, wildlife management and agriculture, such as 'culling a herd'. It can also mean selecting the best items from a group, like culling photos. Using it for people can sound cold, so be careful.

distinctions.note: 'Select' is neutral and positive; 'cull' suggests removing the weaker or unwanted members of a group.
'Kill' is general; 'cull' implies a planned, controlled removal of selected members of a group.

examples.everyday: I'm going to cull my closet this weekend and give away the clothes I never wear.
examples.professional: We need to cull the duplicate records from the customer database before the migration.
examples.analytical: The philosopher warns that any system that culls its members by a single measure of worth will eventually discard what it cannot measure.

nuance.analogy: Culling is like pruning a garden: you cut away what is weak or excess so the rest can grow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin colligere, to collect, through Middle English culle, to pick out.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'cull' with 'call' or 'kill' in pronunciation or meaning.
Using 'cull' for simply picking something up; it implies selection and removal.

senses.definition: To make slightly wet or soiled by spattering or sprinkling a liquid (such as water, mud, or paint) on it; to bedabble.
To cause splashing by moving a body part like a bill or limb in soft mud, water, etc. often playfully; to play in shallow water; to paddle.
senses.example: The children sat on the dock and dabbled their feet in the water.

senses.definition: To feed without diving, by submerging the head and neck underwater to seek food, often also tipping up the tail straight upwards above the water.
To participate or have an interest in an activity in a casual or superficial way.
senses.example: She’s an actress by trade, but has been known to dabble in poetry.

senses.definition: A spattering or sprinkling of a liquid.
An act of splashing in soft mud, water, etc.
An act of participation in an activity in a casual or superficial way.

core.definition: To take part in an activity casually or without serious commitment, or to splash lightly in water or mud.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'l' with a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'DAB-uhl.' Do not add an extra vowel between 'b' and 'l.'

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or neutral; it suggests a casual, shallow involvement rather than serious work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dabble to describe trying an interest or skill without going deep, such as dabbling in painting or cooking. It sounds friendly and modest, and it can be a polite way to say you are not an expert. People might say they 'dabble in the stock market' to signal small, casual investments. Avoid using it for serious professional work, where it can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: Dabble implies casual, light participation, while 'study' or 'work' imply serious, sustained commitment.
Tinker suggests making small adjustments to improve something, while dabble suggests trying something out without depth.

examples.everyday: I dabble in gardening on weekends, but I still buy most of my vegetables at the farmers market.
examples.professional: Our team dabbles in machine learning, but the core product still relies on traditional statistical models.
examples.analytical: Philosophers who only dabble in ethics often miss the deep tensions that specialists have spent decades analyzing.

nuance.analogy: To dabble is like dipping one toe into a lake before deciding whether to swim.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English dabelen, a frequentative of dabben, to splash.
common_mistakes: Using 'dabble on' instead of 'dabble in' with an activity.
Pronouncing it 'DAB-ble' with a clearly pronounced extra vowel.

senses.definition: Appearing as though dead, or on the verge of death.
senses.example: He has a deathly pallor.

senses.definition: Deadly, fatal, causing death.
Extreme.
senses.example: He has a deathly fear of crocodiles.

senses.definition: In a way that resembles death.
senses.example: He was deathly pale.

senses.definition: Extremely, dreadfully.
senses.example: The water was deathly cold.

words.etymology: From Middle English *dethly*, from Old English *dēaþlīċ*, equivalent to *death* + *ly*.

core.definition: Looking as pale, still, or lifeless as a dead person; or extremely great.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the th is voiceless as in breath, so say DETH-lee. The final -ly is a clear, short ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dramatic; it usually describes something frightening, pale, or silent, and the intensifier sense is informal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deathly in phrases like 'deathly pale,' 'deathly silent,' or 'deathly afraid,' which are vivid and often a little exaggerated. The word can sound literary or dramatic in casual speech. It is not used as a plain synonym of deadly, which is more common for fatal things.

distinctions.note: Deadly means capable of causing death, while deathly describes appearance or a state resembling death, or an extreme degree.
Deathlike is a near-synonym that is more literal about resembling death, and is less often used as an intensifier.

examples.everyday: You look deathly pale, so sit down and drink some water before you pass out.
examples.professional: The room went deathly quiet when the CEO announced the layoffs.
examples.analytical: The novel's deathly stillness mirrors the characters' spiritual exhaustion, suggesting a world where hope has already expired.

nuance.analogy: Deathly describes the look and feel of something like a candle that has gone out, with no warmth left.
nuance.etymology: From death, from Old English dēath, plus the adjective suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using deathly for fatal events, as in 'a deathly accident,' where deadly is correct.
Pronouncing the th as a voiced sound like the in this instead of the voiceless sound in breath.

senses.definition: Appropriate social behavior.
A convention of social behavior.

words.etymology: Latin *decōrum*, neuter form of *decōrus* (“proper, decent”).

core.definition: Behavior that is socially correct and suitable for a formal or serious situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'KOR'. The first syllable is a weak 'dih', and the final syllable is a reduced 'uhm', not 'um' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it implies respect and self-control, but can sound stiff if used lightly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'decorum' in formal settings such as courts, legislatures, religious services, or meetings. They often say 'maintain decorum' or 'lose decorum'. In everyday speech, 'manners' or 'behaving yourself' is more common, and 'decorum' may sound overly formal.

distinctions.note: 'Manners' refers to everyday polite behavior, while 'decorum' focuses on behavior suited to a formal occasion.
'Etiquette' is a set of written or customary rules; 'decorum' is the general sense of proper conduct.

examples.everyday: The kids were being silly at the wedding, so their mom reminded them to keep some decorum.
examples.professional: The chair asked everyone to maintain decorum during the budget hearing.
examples.analytical: Decorum is not merely a set of rules but a shared understanding of how people owe one another respect in public life.

nuance.analogy: Decorum is like a stage's curtain: it sets the boundary between public performance and disorder.
nuance.etymology: From Latin decorum, 'that which is proper', neuter of decorus.
common_mistakes: Using 'decorum' for everyday manners where 'manners' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle as 'DEK-or-um'; the first syllable is 'dih'.

senses.definition: Characterized by or causing degeneration.

core.definition: Causing or characterized by a gradual worsening or breakdown of tissue, structure, or function over time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JEN, and the ending -ive is a reduced tiv. Learners often stress the final syllable, but the American stress stays on the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: negative. It describes harmful, progressive decline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use degenerative mainly in medical, scientific, and technical contexts, such as degenerative disease or degenerative arthritis. In everyday speech, people say getting worse over time or progressive. Doctors may use it when describing a condition that slowly gets worse.

distinctions.note: Progressive means getting steadily worse or advancing, while degenerative specifically describes breakdown of tissue or structure.
Chronic means long-lasting, while degenerative means gradually worsening, and a condition can be both.

examples.everyday: My grandmother has a degenerative eye condition, so she needs regular checkups.
examples.professional: The software project showed degenerative performance as the codebase grew without refactoring.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the institution suffers from a degenerative loss of purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow leak in a tire that gets worse until the tire goes flat.
nuance.etymology: From degenerate (verb) plus the adjective suffix -ive, from Latin degenerare.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, as in dih-jen-er-uh-TIV. The stress belongs on the second syllable.
Using degenerative for a sudden event. It refers to a gradual process over time.

senses.definition: A small silver coin issued both during the Roman Republic and during the Roman Empire, equal to 10 asses or 4 sesterces. Roughly one day’s wage for a skilled worker.

words.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *dēnārius*.

core.definition: A small silver coin of ancient Rome, worth about a day's wage for a laborer. The New Testament mentions it in several passages.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NAR, and the final -ius is an unstressed 'us' sound. The plural is denarii (dih-NAR-ee-eye), which Americans rarely use outside Latin classes.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in historical, classical or biblical contexts, such as a sermon, a history class or a Bible study. In conversation it sounds scholarly, so for ordinary money talk say 'dollar' or 'coin'.

distinctions.note: The drachma was the Greek silver coin, while the denarius was Roman; they circulated in overlapping regions but were different currencies.
The shekel was a Hebrew unit of weight and coinage, not a Roman coin, so the two appear in different biblical contexts.
A talent was a large unit of weight or money worth thousands of denarii, not a small coin.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader showed us a picture of a Roman denarius and said it was about a day's pay.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, we compared the denarius in the parable of the vineyard with the modern minimum wage.
examples.analytical: The denarius in Matthew 20:2 functions as a fixed standard of fair payment, which makes the owner's generosity the real subject of the parable.

nuance.analogy: A denarius is like a historical benchmark coin: it tells you what a day's work was worth in that world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin denarius, meaning 'containing ten', from deni, 'ten each', because it originally equaled ten asses.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as 'air' instead of a short 'ih' sound, which the dictionary spelling suggests.
Using 'denarii' as the singular form.
nuance.biblical_note: The denarius is the Roman silver coin named in the Greek New Testament as dēnarion (δηνάριον). Matthew 20:2 describes workers hired for a denarius a day. Matthew 22:19 refers to the coin used to pay the tax to Caesar. Revelation 6:6 cites a denarius as the price of a quart of wheat, which signals scarcity.

senses.definition: An act of disrespect or impiety towards something considered sacred.

words.etymology: From *desecrate* + *ion*.

core.definition: An act of disrespect or violation toward something considered sacred, such as a holy place or object.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on -kray-, and the first syllable has light secondary stress. Pronounce the -tion ending as shun, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals a grave offense against something sacred, and it is strongly condemnatory in news and public debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use desecration in formal settings such as news stories, court cases about graves or religious sites, and public statements. In everyday talk people usually say 'disrespect' or 'damage.' The word carries a heavy moral charge, so reserve it for real sacrilege.

distinctions.note: Sacrilege is the broader term for violating something sacred, and it can be a noun for the offense or the concept. Desecration names a specific act that treats a sacred place or object with contempt.
Vandalism is a legal or everyday term for willful property damage. Desecration implies that the object's sacredness is what has been violated.

collocations: the desecration of a holy site

examples.everyday: My neighbor was furious about the desecration of the old chapel down the street.
examples.professional: The report documented the desecration of several historic churches during the riots, and the city is now planning repairs.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians often distinguished the physical damage done to a shrine from its desecration, which was the loss of the sacred meaning that made the shrine holy.

nuance.analogy: Like a stain on a flag, desecration is damage whose real harm lies in what the object represents.
nuance.etymology: From Latin desecrare (to desecrate), from de- plus sacrare (to consecrate).
common_mistakes: Confusing desecration with decoration, which sounds similar but means something very different.
Placing the stress on the wrong syllable (des-ih-kray-SHUN).

senses.definition: Cunning or deceiving, not straightforward or honest, not frank.

words.etymology: 1590s, "out of the common or direct way," from Latin *devius* (“out of the way, remote, off the main road”), from *de via*, from *de* (“off”) (see *de-*) + *via* (“way, road”).

core.definition: Using clever, dishonest, or indirect methods to deceive or get what one wants; not straightforward or honest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the middle as a quick 'vee' with the vowel reduced. The final syllable is a light 'us', not 'ous' as in 'fabulous'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies dishonesty or scheming, though it can be used with a hint of admiration for cleverness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use devious for people who plot, manipulate, or hide their real aims, such as a devious politician or a devious plan to avoid a bill. It is strong, so do not call a friend devious unless you mean it as an insult or a joke. A milder everyday word is sneaky.

distinctions.note: Sneaky is casual and often about small, petty tricks; devious suggests more planning and cleverness.
Cunning can be neutral or admiring about skill; devious is more clearly negative about deception.

examples.everyday: My little brother has a devious way of getting out of chores.
examples.professional: The vendor's devious pricing made the total cost hard to compare with the other bids.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli's prince often appears devious, yet his method depends on a calculated reading of human weakness.

nuance.analogy: A devious path is like a shortcut through a maze that hides its real destination until you have walked too far.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'devius', meaning out of the way, from 'de-' (away) and 'via' (way).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with three full syllables as DEE-vee-ous.
Confusing devious with 'previous' or 'obvious' in spelling.

senses.definition: Telling people to start eating.

conversation.text: Dinner's ready, everyone; come sit down and dig in!
Don't wait for me; go ahead and dig in while it's hot.
Grandma put the turkey on the table and said, "Dig in!"

core.definition: An informal invitation to start eating, said by a host to guests at a meal.

pronunciation.tip: In this command both words get strong stress, and the vowel in dig is short and quick. Link the words so it sounds like DIG-gin, with the g of dig and the vowel of in blending.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Hosts say this at family dinners, potlucks, and cookouts when food is ready to be served. The usual reply is a quick thanks or just starting to eat. It is friendly and casual, so use it with friends and family, while at a formal dinner a host would more likely say please, help yourselves.

distinctions.note: Help yourself invites guests to take food themselves, while dig in is an encouragement to start eating.
Bon appétit is a French phrase Americans use mainly in restaurants or as a joke; dig in is the everyday American version.

examples.everyday: The food is on the table, so dig in before it gets cold!
examples.professional: After the team lunch was catered, our manager said dig in and we all grabbed plates.
examples.analytical: The phrase dig in works as a speech act that marks the transition from social greeting to shared eating, signaling that the host has finished preparing the meal.

nuance.analogy: Like a starting gun for a race: once it goes off, everyone begins eating together.
nuance.etymology: From dig (Old English dīcian, to dig) plus the particle in, here meaning to begin vigorously.
common_mistakes: Saying the phrase as two separate words with no link, rather than DIG-in with a smooth connection.
Using dig in to mean examine something closely, which is a different sense.

senses.definition: The act of distinguishing between things.
The ability to distinguish between things.
The ability to perceive differences that exist.
The condition of understanding.
Aesthetic discrimination; taste, appreciation.
Perceptiveness.
The ability to make wise judgments; sagacity.
Discretion in judging objectively.

words.etymology: From Middle French *discernement*, equivalent to *discern* + *ment*.

core.definition: The ability to judge well and to perceive the difference between things, especially between what is true or good and what is not.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SURN. The 'nm' cluster is said smoothly, with a small schwa before the final 't', so it sounds like 'dih-SURN-muhnt'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a valued quality of wisdom and judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'discernment' in religious, academic and professional contexts, such as 'use good discernment' or 'spiritual discernment'. In everyday talk, people more often say 'good judgment' or 'common sense'. It sounds respectful and somewhat formal.

distinctions.note: 'Judgment' can mean a verdict or an opinion, while 'discernment' emphasizes the subtle skill of telling things apart.
'Intuition' is a feeling that arrives without reasoning, while 'discernment' implies careful, reflective perception.

examples.everyday: My mom has good discernment when she helps friends decide who to trust.
examples.professional: Good discernment is important when we decide which data quality alerts are truly urgent.
examples.analytical: Discernment requires the ability to distinguish between a genuine good and a merely apparent one.

nuance.analogy: Like a fine sieve that lets the flour through and keeps the lumps out.
nuance.etymology: From 'discern' (Latin discernere, to separate) plus the noun suffix '-ment'.
common_mistakes: Using 'discernment' as a verb; the verb is 'discern'.
Stressing the wrong syllable; it is dih-SURN-ment, not DIS-ser-ment.

senses.definition: One of multiple propositions, any of which, if true, confirm the validity of another proposition (a disjunction).
The state of being disjointed; disjointedness; a disconnect.
Any sentence element that is not fully integrated into the clausal structure of the sentence.
An adverbial that expresses the speaker's or writer's attitude towards, or descriptive statement of, the propositional content of the associated clause or sentence.
A species or population occurring at a distant or separate location, and separated from other members of the same group.
A conjunct of a disjunctive conjunction.
Separate; discontinuous; not connected.
Occurring in widely separated geographic areas.

core.definition: In logic, one of the alternatives in a disjunction; one of the propositions joined by or, any of which can be true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on JUNK, the second syllable. Keep the ending hard with a clear kt sound, and make the vowel in the middle short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used in formal logic and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disjunct almost only in logic, philosophy, and linguistics classes. In general conversation the word is unfamiliar, and people say separate or disconnected. Use it with care in academic writing, where it has a precise meaning.

distinctions.note: A disjunct is one of the parts joined by or; a disjunction is the whole compound statement made of those parts.
A conjunct is one of the parts joined by and; a disjunct is one of the parts joined by or.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure, but I think the second option is the disjunct that matters for this puzzle.
examples.professional: In the rule engine, each disjunct is a separate condition, and the request is approved if any one of them is true.
examples.analytical: If one disjunct is false, the truth of the whole disjunction depends entirely on the remaining disjunct, which is what makes the inference valid.

nuance.analogy: A disjunct is one of several doors into a room; any one of them being open gets you in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin disjunctus, past participle of disjungere, 'to separate'.
common_mistakes: Using disjunct as a general word for separated things in everyday speech.
Confusing disjunct with conjunct, which is the and version.

senses.definition: The act of concealing the truth; hypocrisy or deception.
Hiding one's feelings or intentions.

words.etymology: Middle English *dissimulacioun*, from Old French *dissimulation*, from Latin *dissimulātiō*; equivalent to *dissimule* + *-ation*.

core.definition: The act of hiding your true feelings, motives, or facts behind a false appearance; deception.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on lay, the fourth syllable, and the -shun ending is a short shun sound. The middle syllables are weak, so reduce them to uh.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies hypocrisy or intentional concealment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissimulation in formal writing, religious and philosophical discussion, and literary analysis, and it is rare in casual talk. In everyday speech they would say lying, pretending, or putting on a front. The word has a moral tone, so it fits best when describing deliberate deception rather than a small social pretense.

distinctions.note: Hypocrisy is the gap between what someone says and does, while dissimulation is the act of concealing one's true inner state or intentions.
Deceit is the general term for misleading others, while dissimulation emphasizes concealment through pretense or appearance.

examples.everyday: Telling your boss you love the new schedule when you hate it is a bit of dissimulation, but it keeps the peace.
examples.professional: Dissimulation about the budget will damage our credibility, so we need to report the real numbers.
examples.analytical: Many moral critiques of the court's rhetoric point to dissimulation rather than outright falsehood.

nuance.analogy: Dissimulation is like a stage set: the scene looks real from the audience, but the true structure is hidden behind the painted walls.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissimulatio, from dissimulare 'to conceal, disguise'.
common_mistakes: Using dissimulation as a synonym for simulation, which means imitation or a model.
Stressing the wrong syllable as dis-sih-MYOO-lay-shun.

words.word: Do you need a parking pass?

senses.definition: Asking whether you must pay or register to park.

conversation.text: Do you need a parking pass here on weekends?
Hi, do you need a parking pass for the beach lot?

core.definition: A question asking whether you must buy, register for or display a permit to park in a particular lot or area.

pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo need uh PAR-king pass
pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, the stress falls on 'PARK' (PAR-king), as in most American compounds like 'parking lot'. The 'r' in 'park' is pronounced, and 'pass' is a short 'a' sound, not 'pahs'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a practical question about rules.
nuance.usage_note: Visitors ask this at park entrances, beach offices, trailheads or campus gates. Staff may reply 'Yes, you'll need a day pass from the kiosk' or 'No, parking is free here.' Americans often say 'pass' or 'permit' interchangeably in this context.

distinctions.note: A permit is an official document that allows parking, often for residents or staff; a pass is usually a temporary ticket for visitors.
A ticket is a fine for illegal parking; a pass is what you buy or receive to park legally.

examples.everyday: Do you need a parking pass for the beach? I'm not sure if the lot is free today.
examples.professional: Do you need a parking pass for the campus, or can I use the visitor lot near the lab?
examples.analytical: A parking pass turns a shared public space into a managed resource, so the question reveals who controls access to the lot.

nuance.analogy: Like a ticket for a ride at an amusement park: you need it to get in, and it proves you paid.
common_mistakes: Saying 'parking ticket' for the permit; a parking ticket is a fine.
Putting the stress on 'pass' (pass with a long a) when the compound stress is on the first word.

senses.definition: Characterized by or experiencing no doubt at all, certain; undoubted; undoubting.
Without doubt; certainly; definitely; very probably, in all likelihood; doubtlessly.

words.etymology: From Middle English *douteles*, *dowteles*, equivalent to *doubt* + *less*.

core.definition: Almost certainly; very probably, in all likelihood, and without any real doubt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the b is silent. The middle 'tl' is pronounced quickly, and the final 'less' is reduced to 'lus'.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive, because it expresses confidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use doubtless mostly in writing and formal speech, where it sounds polished but a bit old-fashioned. In casual talk people usually say probably or definitely instead. It is more common as an adjective in phrases like 'a doubtless victory' in literary contexts.

distinctions.note: Undoubtedly is more common in everyday American English and sounds stronger, while doubtless sounds more formal and literary.
Probably is casual and widely used for likelihood, while doubtless expresses a stronger sense of near-certainty.

examples.everyday: You're doubtless exhausted after that long flight, so get some rest.
examples.professional: The vendor will doubtless push back on the timeline, so we should prepare our data before the meeting.
examples.analytical: The author doubtless intended the ambiguity, since the passage supports several readings of the central claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a bright sunrise that you do not need to question before you see it.
nuance.etymology: From doubt, plus the suffix -less, meaning without doubt.
common_mistakes: Using 'doubtlessly', which is possible but less standard than 'doubtless'.
Using doubtless in casual conversation where probably is more natural.

senses.definition: To make dry.
To become dry.
To cease milking a cow in preparation for calving.

conversation.text: Dry off before you get in the car, please.
The kids came out of the pool and dried off in the sun.
Here's a towel so you can dry off.

core.definition: To make something or someone dry, or to become dry, especially after being wet from water.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on "off," which is the primary stress, and "dry" has a lighter secondary stress. Do not stress both words equally, and keep the ɔ vowel of "caught" in most American speech.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a practical, everyday phrase.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dry off after swimming, showering, or washing a pet, as in "Go dry off before you get cold." It is informal and natural in family and casual speech. A common reply is "I'm drying off, I'll be right out" or simply "Okay."

distinctions.note: Dry out often means to become dry after a long period of wetness or to stop drinking alcohol, while dry off is about removing water from a wet body or surface.
Dry is a general word for removing moisture, while dry off usually refers to a person or animal after water contact.

collocations: take a minute to dry off

examples.everyday: Hurry up and dry off with that towel before you catch a cold after the pool.
examples.professional: Our field crew dries off the equipment before it goes back into the storage van.
examples.analytical: In Leviticus, the priests must wash and dry off before they enter the holy place, marking a boundary between clean and unclean.

nuance.analogy: Drying off is like wringing out a sponge until the last drops are gone and it feels light again.
nuance.etymology: Dry comes from Old English drȳge; off from Old English of.
common_mistakes: Saying "dry up" for drying a wet body, which means something else such as ending or shrinking.
Forgetting the particle; say dry off, not "dry" alone when you mean removing water from a person.

senses.definition: Black in color.
Having dark skin; black.
Made of ebony.
(now poetic) Ebony; an ebony tree.

words.etymology: From Old French *eban* (modern *ébène*), from Latin *ebenus*, from Ancient Greek *ἔβενος* (“ebony tree”).

core.definition: Literary word meaning black or very dark, as in ebon night or ebon hair.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, not a full vowel. Say it as 'EB-un', not 'ee-BON'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly poetic; it sounds elevated and lovely, so it suits poetry or vivid description rather than everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use ebon in conversation. You will meet it in poetry, fantasy writing or fancy description, such as an ebon sky. In ordinary speech say black or dark.

distinctions.note: Black is the everyday word for the color; ebon is an elevated, poetic synonym.
Ebony is the dark wood, or a deep black used in ordinary speech, as in an ebony piano; ebon is the poetic adjective.

examples.everyday: Her grandmother had ebon hair when she was young, and she still tells that story like a fairy tale.
examples.professional: The marketing brief called the car's finish ebon, but the dealer's catalog just says black.
examples.analytical: Milton's ebon night is less a literal color than a symbol of chaos and the absence of divine light.

nuance.analogy: Ebon is the velvet version of black, a word that makes darkness sound deliberate and beautiful.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ebene, via Latin ebenus and Greek ebenos, meaning ebony wood.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two full syllables, like EE-bone
Using ebon in everyday speech where black sounds natural

senses.definition: The tendency to think selfishly with exclusive self-interest in mind.
The belief that moral behavior should be directed toward one's self-interest only.
Egotism (tendency to talk excessively about oneself).

words.etymology: From French *égoïsme*, from New Latin *egoismus*, from Latin *ego*.

core.definition: Selfishness; the belief or habit of acting mainly in one's own interest, or the view that self-interest is the basis of morality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EE. The final syllable is a reduced 'um', and the 'i' in the second syllable is short.

nuance.connotation: Negative in everyday use, suggesting selfishness; neutral in philosophy, where it names a theory.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use egoism mostly in philosophy classes, ethics debates, or formal writing about character. In everyday speech, people say 'selfishness' or 'self-interest'. Be careful: egoism can mean a moral theory, while egotism means excessive talk about oneself.

distinctions.note: Egotism means talking too much about yourself or boasting, while egoism means putting your own interests first in action or morality.
Selfishness is the everyday word for refusing to share or help, while egoism is a more formal term, often used for a theory or principle.

examples.everyday: That kind of egoism is why he never helps with the dishes.
examples.professional: Her approach to negotiating is pure egoism, so she rarely considers the other side's interests.
examples.analytical: Ethical egoism claims that acting for one's own benefit is the only rational basis for morality, a position many critics find hard to defend.

nuance.analogy: Egoism is like a compass that points only to your own interests, ignoring the road others are traveling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ego, I, plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using egoism to mean talking about oneself too much; that meaning belongs to egotism.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'eg' instead of 'EE'.

senses.definition: The materialist view that the majority of the mental states assumed by common sense like belief or sensation do not exist.

core.definition: The philosophical view that common-sense mental states such as beliefs and sensations do not really exist and should be replaced by neuroscience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIM in eliminative and on TEER in materialism. Keep the first syllable of materialism reduced to a schwa and do not stress it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a term from philosophy of mind and often sounds provocative to people outside the field.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in philosophy of mind and cognitive science courses and debates. It is often shortened to eliminativism in discussion. Outside academic settings people would describe the idea more plainly, for example by saying that folk psychology is wrong.

distinctions.note: Physicalism holds that everything is physical, but it can accept that mental states exist; eliminative materialism denies that many common mental states exist.
Identity theory says mental states are identical to brain states; eliminative materialism says the folk mental states are false and should be dropped.

examples.everyday: My roommate got into a long argument about whether beliefs are real, and he kept bringing up eliminative materialism.
examples.professional: Our cognitive science team discussed eliminative materialism when we debated whether we should model beliefs at all.
examples.analytical: Eliminative materialism claims that folk psychological categories such as belief and desire will be replaced by neuroscientific ones, rather than reduced to them.

nuance.analogy: It is like saying the old word for a disease does not name a real thing, so doctors should use the precise biological terms instead.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the late twentieth century from eliminate, materialism and related philosophical terms.
common_mistakes: Stressing materialism on the second syllable, as in muh-TEER-ee-uh-liz-um rather than mat-EER-ee-uh-liz-um.
Confusing eliminative materialism with ordinary materialism, which only says everything is physical.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being emollient; soothingness; softness.
The act of soothing or appeasing; mollification.

core.definition: The quality of being soft, soothing or gentle, either physically on the skin or in manner and effect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MAHL. The last syllable is a reduced 'uhns', not a strong 'ance'. The middle syllables are quick and light, so the word sounds like 'ih-MAHL-yuhns'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes softness or soothing quality, and it is mostly used in careful or technical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'emollience' in conversation. It appears mainly in scientific, medical or literary writing about skin products or gentle styles. In everyday speech, people say 'softness' or 'soothing' instead.

distinctions.note: Emollience is the abstract quality, while an emollient is the substance or the soothing thing itself.
Softness is the everyday word for something that is not hard, while emollience emphasizes a soothing or moisturizing effect.

examples.everyday: I love how the lotion has such gentle emollience that my hands don't feel dry anymore.
examples.professional: The cosmetics team tested the formula for emollience, and it scored well on skin softness and comfort.
examples.analytical: The poem's emollience lies in its slow rhythms, which soften the harsh political subject without concealing it.

nuance.analogy: Emollience is like a warm blanket for the skin or mood: it smooths out roughness and makes things feel gentler.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'emollire', to soften, from 'mollis', soft.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'emolument', which means payment or benefit from a job.
Stressing the last syllable: say 'ih-MAHL-yuhns', not 'ih-mahl-YANTS'.

senses.definition: To invigorate; to make energetic.
To supply with energy, especially electricity; to turn on power to (something).
senses.example: Whenever we energize that circuit we blow a fuse.

words.etymology: From *energy* + *-ize*.

core.definition: To give someone or something new energy, or to make them feel more active and lively.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a single 'ize' sound that rhymes with 'eyes,' not a separate 'eyes' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a boost of enthusiasm or vitality, though in technical contexts it can be neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use energize for people, teams, and crowds, as in 'The coffee energized me.' In technical or household contexts, 'turn on' or 'power up' is more common for electronics. In a meeting, saying 'Let's energize the team' sounds natural but a little motivational.

distinctions.note: Motivate focuses on giving someone a reason to act; energize focuses on giving them more vitality or enthusiasm.
Invigorate is more formal and often describes refreshing the body or mind; energize is more common in everyday speech.
Power refers to supplying electricity or force to a device; energize can be used this way too, but in ordinary speech it is more often about people.

examples.everyday: A quick walk after lunch always energizes me before the afternoon.
examples.professional: The new product launch energized the whole sales team and gave us a clear goal for next quarter.
examples.analytical: The sacramental liturgy, in this account, energizes the community by reconnecting it to the source of its life.

nuance.analogy: Energizing someone is like plugging a phone into a charger: the battery goes from low to full.
nuance.etymology: From energy, plus the verb-forming suffix -ize, from Greek -izein.
common_mistakes: Using 'energize' with the wrong stress pattern, saying 'en-er-JIZE' instead of 'EN-er-jyze.'
Confusing energize with energetic; say 'The speech energized the crowd' rather than 'The speech was energetic the crowd.'

senses.definition: To trust to the care of.
senses.example: Can I entrust you with a secret?

core.definition: To give someone responsibility for something important, trusting them to take care of it well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The first syllable is 'in,' not 'en,' and the r is a clean American r.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it shows confidence and respect in the person given the responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entrust for serious responsibilities such as money, secrets, children, or a company. For ordinary tasks, people say put someone in charge of something or trust someone with it. The usual patterns are entrust something to someone and entrust someone with something.

distinctions.note: Trust is a feeling or belief; entrust is the act of handing over something valuable to someone's care.
Delegate means assigning tasks at work; entrust carries a stronger sense of personal responsibility for something precious.

examples.everyday: I entrusted my dog to my neighbor while we were on vacation.
examples.professional: The director entrusted the migration plan to the senior engineer, who had handled the last two.
examples.analytical: Institutions survive when they entrust authority to people who can be held accountable for how they use it.

nuance.analogy: Entrusting something is like handing someone a key to your house: you give them access because you believe they will use it well.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English entrusten, from en- plus trust.
common_mistakes: Using entrust for small everyday tasks, which sounds overly dramatic.
Omitting the preposition: say entrust something to someone or entrust someone with something.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the key idea is that God or the gospel is entrusted to people, who must faithfully keep it. The Greek words behind it are pisteuō (to believe, to be entrusted with) and parathēkē (a deposit or thing entrusted to another for safekeeping). Romans 3:2 says the Jewish people were entrusted with the oracles of God, meaning they had the privilege and duty of guarding God's revealed word. 1 Timothy 1:11 describes Paul as entrusted with the gospel of God's glory. 2 Timothy 1:14 urges Timothy to guard the deposit that has been entrusted to him, relying on the Holy Spirit who dwells within.

senses.definition: The condition of a system in which competing influences are balanced, resulting in no net change.
Mental balance.
1 2 “equilibrium” listed in the Oxford English Dictionary [2 Ed.]
The state of a reaction in which the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are the same.
The state of a body at rest or in uniform motion in which the resultant of all forces on it is zero.

words.etymology: From Latin *aequilībrium*, from *aequus* + *lībra* (“balance”).

core.definition: A state in which opposing forces or influences are balanced, so there is no net change.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIB. Pronounce the r clearly in the American style, and keep the final -um weak. Do not say lib-rium with a silent middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests stability, though it can also describe a stalemate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use equilibrium in science, economics and everyday talk about emotional balance, as in trying to find your equilibrium after a hard week. It is fairly formal but widely understood. In casual speech people often say balance.

distinctions.note: Balance is everyday and can refer to physical or mental states; equilibrium emphasizes a stable state where opposing forces cancel out.
Stability means resistance to change; equilibrium describes a state of balance that may itself be dynamic.

examples.everyday: After the big fight, it took her a few weeks to get her emotional equilibrium back.
examples.professional: The team's staffing model reached equilibrium once the new hires matched the number of people leaving.
examples.analytical: Many economic models describe prices as adjusting until supply and demand reach an equilibrium.

nuance.analogy: Like a seesaw with equal weights on both ends, it stays level.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aequilibrium (equal balance), from aequus (equal) and libra (scales, balance).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle as a silent lib-rium without the American r.
Using equilibrium for a single object when balance is more natural.

senses.definition: A person who estimates, especially one who estimates costs.
A function of a random sample of a population used to estimate some parameter of the whole population.

words.etymology: From Latin *aestimātor*; equivalent to *estimate* + *or*.

core.definition: In statistics, a rule or formula that uses sample data to compute an estimate of a population parameter.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel. The final '-or' is a reduced 'er' sound in American speech, so don't say 'estimator' with a full 'oh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In statistics, an 'estimator' is the function applied to data, distinct from the numerical result. In everyday business language, an 'estimator' is a person who prepares cost estimates, especially in construction and engineering. Both meanings are used, so context tells you which one is meant.

distinctions.note: An estimator is the formula or the person doing the estimating; an estimate is the result it produces.
The estimator is the procedure; the estimand is the target quantity being estimated.

examples.everyday: My cousin works as an estimator for a roofing company, so she's always measuring houses to price jobs.
examples.professional: We should use the sample mean as our estimator, since it is unbiased and easy to explain to the product team.
examples.analytical: An estimator is consistent if, as the sample grows, its values converge in probability to the true parameter.

nuance.analogy: An estimator is like a recipe: it specifies how to combine the ingredients (the data) to get the dish (the estimate), and different recipes give different results.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'estimate' with the agent suffix '-or,' meaning 'one who estimates.'
common_mistakes: Using 'estimator' as a synonym for 'estimate' when speaking about a result rather than a method.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'or' rather than the American reduced 'er.'

senses.definition: A person who performs evil acts.

words.etymology: From Middle English *yvel doer*; equivalent to *evil* + *doer*.

core.definition: A person who deliberately does evil or wicked things, especially someone who harms others.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, and the second part, 'doer,' has a weak secondary stress. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'EE-vul' quickly, not 'EE-vool.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it names a person who does wrong, and it often carries moral judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evildoer in religious, moral and political speech, and sometimes in news or political commentary. It sounds dramatic in everyday conversation, so people usually say 'bad guy' or 'criminal' instead. It is common in sermons and Bible study.

distinctions.note: A criminal breaks the law, while an evildoer is a moral term that may apply to anyone who does wicked things, whether or not they are illegal.
'Wrongdoer' is milder and more general, while 'evildoer' is stronger and implies deliberate malice.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always said that justice catches up with evildoers, even if it takes years.
examples.professional: In the leadership talk, I said that we must hold evildoers accountable, but we also need fair processes.
examples.analytical: The psalmist's lament names the evildoers as those whose prosperity seems to undermine trust in God's justice.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire starter in a village: the damage is deliberate, not an accident.
nuance.etymology: From evil plus doer, one who does; the compound is English.
common_mistakes: Writing 'evil doer' as two words in formal writing; the standard form is 'evildoer.'
Using 'evildoer' for minor mistakes; it is too strong for ordinary wrongdoing.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the word is often mēʿrîm or related forms from the root pāʿal or rāʿa, meaning to do evil or act wickedly. In Greek, 1 Peter 4:15 uses kakopoios, 'doer of evil.' Psalm 37:1 tells believers not to fret over evildoers, and 1 Peter 4:15 warns Christians not to suffer as an evildoer. Psalm 92:7 says the wicked sprout like grass but are doomed to destruction.

senses.definition: To dig out of the ground; to take out of a place of burial; to disinter.
senses.example: The archeologist exhumed artifacts from the ground with a shovel.

senses.definition: To uncover; to bring to light.
senses.example: Long dead traditions are exhumed just for the tourists.

words.etymology: From Medieval Latin *exhumō*, from Latin *ex-* + *humō* (“to bury”).

core.definition: To dig up a buried body or object, or to bring a forgotten past event or idea back into public attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -hyoom. The initial 'ex' is pronounced 'eks' and the 'h' is often dropped in casual speech to 'eks-YOOM', so both are acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds serious and is often used in news, legal or historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exhume most often for digging up a body for legal, forensic or historical reasons, and in news reports about cemeteries or famous figures. In a figurative sense, it means bringing forgotten facts or old ideas back to light, as in a history article. Ordinary speakers would normally say 'dig up' for everyday digging.

distinctions.note: Dig up is everyday and general, while exhume is formal and typically used for graves, bodies or buried records.
Disinter is a precise, formal synonym, mostly for bodies; exhume is more common and more flexible in figurative use.

examples.everyday: The news said they might exhume the old family grave to run a DNA test.
examples.professional: The research team wants to exhume the old project archives to see why the first model failed.
examples.analytical: The historian aims to exhume the forgotten debates that shaped the early church councils.

nuance.analogy: To exhume is like archaeology on a single spot: you carefully bring something hidden back into the light.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exhumare, from ex- 'out of' plus humus 'ground'.
common_mistakes: Using 'exhume' for ordinary digging, such as in a garden, which sounds odd.
Pronouncing the initial 'ex' as 'ig' in all contexts; 'ek' or 'eks' is more common in American usage.

senses.definition: To reveal; to uncover; to make visible; to bring to light.
To subject photographic film to light, thereby recording an image.
To submit to an active (mostly dangerous) substance, such as radiation, a chemical, or any other stress.
senses.example: Residents were exposed to dangerous levels of radiation.

senses.definition: To make available to other parts of a program, or to other programs.
senses.example: to expose an API

senses.definition: To abandon, especially an unwanted baby in the wilderness.

words.etymology: From Middle English *exposen*, from Old French *exposer* (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin *expōnō* (“set forth”), with contamination from *poser* (“to lay, place”).

core.definition: To reveal something that was hidden, or to make someone experience something harmful or unpleasant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SPOHZ, and the final z is voiced, so it sounds like the word goes. Learners often add a vowel before the s cluster, so say it as one smooth syllable.

nuance.connotation: Often negative when it means revealing wrongdoing or putting someone at risk; neutral or positive when it means revealing the truth or showing something to others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expose in news, everyday talk and science, as in 'The report exposed the company's mistakes.' In casual speech it can also mean exposing yourself to something harmful, such as the sun. A natural reply is to ask what was revealed or how serious the exposure was.

distinctions.note: Reveal is neutral and general, while expose often implies that the thing was hidden on purpose and is now shown as wrong.
Uncover emphasizes removing a covering, while expose stresses making something harmful or secret visible.

examples.everyday: Don't expose the bread dough to cold air for too long, or it won't rise well.
examples.professional: The security audit exposed a flaw in our authentication logic that we need to patch this sprint.
examples.analytical: The essay exposes the hidden assumptions behind the argument, showing how the conclusion depends on contested premises.

nuance.analogy: To expose something is like pulling back a curtain so that what was behind it can be seen.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exponere, to put out or set forth.
common_mistakes: Using expose with the wrong preposition, saying expose at instead of expose to when talking about risk.
Confusing expose with exposure, the noun.

senses.definition: An object serving as a simplified interface to a larger body of code, as in the facade pattern.
The face or front (most visible side) of any other thing, such as the prospect of an organ.
A deceptive or insincere outward appearance.
The face of a building, especially the front view or elevation.
To cover or disguise an outward appearance.

words.etymology: French *façade*, from Italian *facciata*, a derivation of *faccia* (“front”), from Latin *faciēs* (“face”); compare *face*.

core.definition: A false or superficial appearance that hides the true nature of a person, situation or organization.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SAHD. The final e is silent, and the vowel is the same open vowel as in 'father' in General American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses, because it suggests hiding the truth. Neutral when describing the front of a building.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use facade for a false front, such as someone's calm public face hiding anxiety, or a company covering up problems. It is more formal and vivid than fake or front. In architecture, it means the face of a building, which is a neutral use.

distinctions.note: Front is neutral and general, while facade often suggests something deceptive hiding what lies beneath.
A mask is worn over the face, while a facade is a broader, more constructed appearance that hides reality.
Pretense is the act of pretending, while facade is the visible result that conceals the truth.

examples.everyday: Her cheerful facade fooled everyone, but she was struggling badly after the move.
examples.professional: Our status deck was a facade of progress; the real blockers were in the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Many critics argue that political rhetoric builds a facade of consensus that hides deep disagreement.

nuance.analogy: A facade is like a movie set's painted storefront: convincing from the street, but empty behind the door.
nuance.etymology: From French facade, from Italian facciata, from faccia, 'face,' from Latin facies.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'side' instead of the silent-e pattern; it is fuh-SAHD.
Using facade only for buildings; in American speech it usually means a false front.

senses.definition: Existing only in the fancy (“imagination”) or by social convention; imaginary, imagined; supposed; perceived rather than real.
